Oh, by the way, as we continue to gain share, the variable gross margin is quite good. As I said, we also believe there's going to be some COVID in 2023. It's hard to size it right now, but it's not going to go away anytime soon.
Mark Guinan
CFO, Quest Diagnostics
Yeah. Then the other thing, Pito, is I mean, you know I'm not in any position to provide guidance in 2023. That's why we're focusing everyone on the base business. However, when you think about what could happen, COVID could be larger. We don't know. We're not counting at this point. Then we did mention we expect to have $1 billion of cash this year.
Between opportunity to do quite a bit of M&A, and we'll see or do share repurchases, those also aren't specifically contemplated. That's why locking down to a specific number is really difficult and probably not productive. So I would point you to what we said on Investor Day and kind of assuming that that's reasonable if these things don't play out significantly differently from our current view of what 2023 might bring.
Pito Chickering
Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Great. Thanks so much, guys.
Shawn Bevec
VP of Investor Relations, Quest Diagnostics
Operator, next question.
Operator
And the next question is coming from Matt Larew of William Blair. Your line is open.
Matt Larew
Partner, William Blair
Hi. Good morning. The 3% Invigorate target has been aided in recent years as you've consolidated a volume onto your two new labs and consolidated onto one immunoassay platform. I'm curious, what are the keys going forward here to keep driving those gains?
And then maybe the second piece on costs would be separate from some of the extra costs you've called out today related to COVID. Clearly, you built up some infrastructure, both personnel and instrumentation for COVID. And just curious, how much of that do you think goes away as COVID moves to an endemic and perhaps you need less extra capacity?
Stephen Rusckowski
Chairman, CEO, and President, Quest Diagnostics
Great. Thanks for the question. I'll start. I'm going to turn it to Jim to add to it. But we've been working on operational excellence for over a decade. It has become institutionalized in our company culture and embedded in how we do things. It is a platform for how we're going to continue to grow. Your comment was around cost.
We don't talk about cost. We talk about productivity because there's a lot of aspects of what we do around Invigorate. Some actually helps the top line. Some actually helps getting more output with less labor. Yes, some helps us become more efficient by less input from some of the materials that we use.
So we look at it in aggregate. We continue to be bullish on our prospects. We believe that it is the ingredients for us to continue to deliver great value. That is, when we do this, we improve our quality, our service gets better. And oh, by the way, we become more and more productive to be able to make the investments to fuel the growth. It all fits together.
Then when we talk about this, when we talked about it on Investor Day, we see an enormous opportunity for us to continue to digitize and innovate in operational excellence. So some of you have had the opportunity to tour through our latest lab of the future. That's our new facility in Clifton, New Jersey. Sometime, if you come in, you'll see what we've done.
We've taken some of the learning out of our Marlborough facility up in the Boston area. We've brought that down to Clifton, and we built on it. And that also uses the advantages of some consolidation with some of our new platforms. But Jim and team are now taking that and thinking about, okay, what's next? Okay? When you think about innovation in our space, yes, there's innovation in terms of testing and as far as diagnostic information services.
But we equally think there's a lot of innovation and opportunity for us to move forward. We continue to invest. And when we talk about investments, we talk about the use of cash. As you noticed, we've been putting about $400 million a year into our capital budget, which is investments and, frankly, a lot of our innovation that allow us to fuel this productivity gain. Jim, add to that, please.
Jim Davis
EVP of General Diagnostics and CEO-Elect, Quest Diagnostics
Yeah. I think Steve touched on the three key themes: automation, the use of artificial intelligence, and then the continued digitization of so many of our manual processes. So Marlborough and Clifton are terrific examples of that. But as you know, they're all brand new laboratories. We've got 20+ other laboratories in our network. And there's opportunities in every one of those laboratories without building new greenfield sites to continue that automation journey.
In particular, in our specimen processing area and in what we call our fluid handling system, handling of blood and urine. On the artificial intelligence side, you're going to see us move in pathology, cytology, microbiology. We've got some great examples in each of those departments today. We're deploying artificial intelligence systems to help with the readout of those images. And then, as Steve mentioned, just the continued digitization.
Now, beyond the immunoassay platform where we consolidated around the Atellica, there are still other opportunities like that in our laboratories. We recently ran a competition in urinalysis, selected a new vendor, Sysmex, for that platform. And rolling out those new platforms across all 23+ laboratories is going to generate a lot of productivity year-over-year. As long as we have healthy third-party vendors that continue to innovate, those innovations will come to our labs. And we'll continue along that 3% productivity journey.
Stephen Rusckowski
Chairman, CEO, and President, Quest Diagnostics
Yeah. We're bullish on the prospects of continuing to drive productivity. I always react to, this is a cost-cutting goal. And this is not about a cost-cutting goal. This is about working smarter. And this has been a key part of our strategy. And it fuels growth. And Jim mentioned some of the areas.
I mentioned my interest in common also digital pathology, which will revolutionize our ability to diagnose, treat, and do that more productively. As a matter of fact, this week, Jim is going out to another laboratory and taking a look at where we're going to make our next investment this year. We're going to continue to invest in this space. We think there's a lot more opportunity in front of us. It's exciting.
Mark Guinan
CFO, Quest Diagnostics
Yeah, I just want to add that remember, this is not just in the lab. There's a lot of productivity that's driven outside. Specifically, I'll give two examples of logistics. We really have an incredible ability to be efficient with logistics. It's continuing to improve. We have some cases where we have empty pickups, where we have some customers that don't give us specimens all the time.
It's periodic. Now we have the ability and technology to not do that empty pickup. So that's an efficiency. We also get requests for what we call staff pickups, where somebody needs something quick, quick turnaround, etc. And so the ability to most efficiently get one of our vehicles there has been enhanced through our technology. The other one is in our patient draw centers. We've really increasingly moved the administrative burdens off the phlebotomists, allowed them to do phlebotomy by getting people to go to our website, put in their insurance information, everything.
And so if our phlebotomist can spend a couple less minutes with each patient doing administrative work and doing phlebotomy, we drive up the productivity in our draw centers. Those are just a couple examples of productivity gains that aren't really cost reductions, but enhance our ability to do more with the same resources and drive up our quality and everything else outside the laboratory.
Shawn Bevec
VP of Investor Relations, Quest Diagnostics
Operator, next question, please.
Operator
And the next question is coming from Tycho Peterson of JPMorgan. Your line is open.
[Analyst] (JPMorgan)
Analyst, JPMorgan
Hi, guys. This is Casey on for Tycho. Congratulations to all. Can you maybe talk towards the percentage of COVID testing that was consumer-initiated in Q4, whether through QuestDirect or other non-traditional avenues? And how do you see that trending in 2022? You mentioned that there are different costs associated with non-traditional avenues of testing. Maybe can you quantify the difference in margin profiles between traditional and non-traditional?
Mark Guinan
CFO, Quest Diagnostics
Yeah. What I can share is, I go back to what we said in the prepared remarks. Our consumer business was about $70 million last year between the base and COVID. We did $2.7 billion of COVID revenue. The consumer-initiated COVID testing was very small at this point. And it's strengthening. And again, as I said, we continue to enhance our website when people go for that ordering and testing and so on.
But there's still more to come in terms of enhancing that experience for consumers and driving awareness for people. As you know, we're competing with a lot of people who see these stand-up operations in parking lots and so on and so forth, which draw their attention. We're working on making sure that they know we can do this if they initiate themselves as opposed to going to a doctor or a hospital for this.
We expect to get stronger and stronger moving forward as we enhance our overall consumer business through these investments we just mentioned. In terms of the margin profile, it's really not all that different between the consumer. And consumer can add in different ways. They can come to our patient draw center and have it done there. We do have home collection kits where they can be sent to their home. A little different structure, but not materially different in profitability.
Shawn Bevec
VP of Investor Relations, Quest Diagnostics
Operator, next question.
Operator
The next question is coming from Derik de Bruin of Bank of America. Your line is open.
Derik de Bruin
Analyst, Bank of America
Hey, great. Thank you for squeezing me in. I'll just make this quick. Can we talk a little bit about sort of the real PAMA outlook? You would assume $80 million hit again comes back in 2023. What are the chances that this actually does get resolved and that the lobbying efforts pay off? Is the current administration a little bit more and Congress a little bit more willing to sort of listen to this and sort of deal with it? I mean, is there a chance that there's actually some reversion just given what happened? Thanks.
Mark Guinan
CFO, Quest Diagnostics
Yeah. Before Steve addresses that, I just want to remind everybody that that $80 million was built into our long-term outlook. We just assumed it would happen this year. Again, although it will be a year-on-year hit to us incrementally in comparison, in the long-term outlook, it was assumed that we would get that in 2022. It's already built in. Go ahead, Steve.
Stephen Rusckowski
Chairman, CEO, and President, Quest Diagnostics
Yeah. Thanks for the question. As we said, we were thankful that it was delayed again, the one-year offset as Mark indicated to 2023. We think that's good for us because it will gain us some time this year to keep on working on a permanent fix with Congress. We have been very active working with Congress last year. As you know, Congress was very busy with the infrastructure bill, and other business. Therefore, we were fortunate enough to get in the postponement of PAMA.
But it allows us time this year to keep on working on this to get appropriate effects. We're encouraged by the level of support. The good news is about the pandemic has brought front and center the importance of testing, the importance of having a strong industry. We're getting strong bipartisan support both from the House and from the Senate.
We made a proposal of what we think should be changed to improve the data collection process, the sampling of market-based data. We continue to support the notion and the philosophy of PAMA, that is, we should be paid a commercial rate. But we believe that CMS got it wrong.
And in parallel with the work we're doing with Congress, we continue to have our lawsuit against CMS as a trade association. The judge has heard the arguments. We'll see if we get some indication on a decision on that. Hard to call that. But that's still in the works as well. Our work right now this year is to push for a permanent fix to PAMA.
And we're better positioned now because of the pandemic than before the pandemic because of the strength of this industry in full awareness and appreciation of what we've done and the need for a strong laboratory industry going forward.
Shawn Bevec
VP of Investor Relations, Quest Diagnostics
Operator, last question, please.
Operator
And our last question is coming from Eric Coldwell of Baird. Your line is open.
Stephen Rusckowski
Chairman, CEO, and President, Quest Diagnostics
Hey, Eric.
Eric Coldwell
Senior Analyst, Baird
Hey. Good morning. Thank you. Masterful job clearing up some of the overriding concerns on core markets today. So thank you. When you went through your list of things that don't repeat or go down significantly as COVID incremental cost over time, staffing challenges, etc., go away, you mentioned bonuses. And I think it was the one number in the list of callouts that I didn't hear you quantify.
I'm curious if we could get the incremental bonus due to the COVID upside profitability in 2021, how you think that bonus will normalize, whether it's 2022 or 2023. And then my follow-up, I'll just throw it in here. I was hoping we could get average-weighted reimbursement in Q4. I know you said it would be relatively similar through the PHE, but if you could give us a little more specificity on where AWR came out in Q4 on COVID PCR testing, that would be helpful. Thanks.
Mark Guinan
CFO, Quest Diagnostics
Sure. Let me start with that one because I think there were some questions around maybe whether turnaround time suffered and we didn't get the $25 fee that comes with some of the government payers, a couple of the commercial payers. And actually, not really. AWR in Q4 was absolutely similar to what it has been in the previous quarters.
Our turnaround time performance was outstanding. In January, when the surge came, we did have a little bit of a hit to our turnaround times. But obviously, that's all contemplated in the guidance that we just provided and everything. It wasn't a huge amount. When you go back to the early question on the bonuses, when you look at the bonuses, most of it is really our 50,000 employees.
People think about, oh, bonuses must be senior management. But most of the cost is really we pay a 3% bonus to even our wage workers. And then obviously, we have other staff members that have higher targets. And every year, we budget for what we call 1X, whatever that target is. For most of the people, it'd be 3%.
And based on performance, and we feel we've had reasonably stretched performances when you list historically, we have not paid significantly above 1X. And we've had a number of years where it's been low 1X. But the COVID unpredictability and the surge in revenues enabled us to pay our employees significant bonuses in 2020 and again in 2021.
And so if you look at, without getting too specific, we've shared a number in the past of $3 billion wage bill that's gone up in the last couple of years as we've grown the company. You can kind of, as a floor, say 3%, obviously a little higher because there's people who are on a higher bonus. That's about 1X. And then we're paying a bonus that's substantially higher than that in 2021 like we did in 2020.
The other thing is we did pay out a $500 payment to a majority of our employees to compensate them for COVID expenses. In 2020, we adjusted it out of our adjusted earnings because we were seeing COVID as temporal and extraordinary. But once you get to your second time doing it, even though I still think it's extraordinary, we just decided not to adjust it out.
We did have over a $20 million payment late in the year, $500 to our wage employees and some of our lower compensated professionals as well. Those are a couple of things that would go away and not be repeated unless somehow we had another surprising COVID year in 2022 like we had in 2020 and 2021.
Eric Coldwell
Senior Analyst, Baird
Okay. Great response. I'm not sure I'm smart enough to do 1X, 3%+, and then significant increases. Is there any chance you could frame that as an incremental $50 million, incremental $100 million? I'm just directionally, could we get a little closer?
Mark Guinan
CFO, Quest Diagnostics
Yeah. Let's say it's less than $100 million, but substantially more than $50 million.
Eric Coldwell
Senior Analyst, Baird
Okay. That's about what I thought. Okay. Thank you very much, guys. Congrats to everyone.
Stephen Rusckowski
Chairman, CEO, and President, Quest Diagnostics
Thank you. Very good. Well, thanks. It's been a good session with you all. Thanks for all the great questions. And again, thanks for joining the call today. And we appreciate your support. You guys have a great day.
